items.q: Which materials make smoke that is hardest for a station smoke detector to see?
items.a: In NASA's SAME-2 flight experiment, Kapton made the finest smoke of the five materials tested: a geometric mean diameter of 42 nm unaged (89 nm after 12 minutes of aging), followed by Teflon at 81 nm. Using the paper's own size spreads, about 82% of Kapton's smoke mass is in particles finer than 500 nm, against 9% for silicone. Light-scattering detectors like the station's respond weakly to particles that fine, so Kapton and Teflon smoke is the hardest to see. The paper says the small Kapton and Teflon particles will make detection challenging for light scattering devices.

sources.label: Urban et al. 2012, SAME-2 particle sizes, AIAA 2012-3536 (NASA NTRS 20130000422), Table 1

items.q: How fast does air move inside the space station?
items.a: NASA's requirement for the space station is an effective air velocity in the cabin aisleway of 4.6 to 12.2 metres per minute, which is about 0.08 to 0.2 metres per second. With no buoyancy, smoke and heat go wherever the ventilation carries them instead of rising.

sources.label: Link and Balistreri, ISS inter-module ventilation, ICES 2015 (NASA NTRS 20150009509), p. 10

items.q: How fast will a fire spread on the Moon?
items.a: No NASA evidence. The NASA archive we use has no combustion data taken at lunar gravity. Microgravity and Earth-gravity results can bound the answer, but we do not predict a value in between.

sources.label: Challenge brief: no partial-gravity combustion data in PSI
